prompt: According to the lesson, what does a DLP tool mostly stop?

choices.text: Mistakes
choices.why: Right: a spreadsheet mailed home, a file on a converter site.

choices.text: Intruders who broke into the network from outside
choices.why: That is the business of the other lessons; DLP starts from people allowed to read the data.

choices.text: Determined insiders, who cannot get round it
choices.why: A determined person can photograph the screen.

choices.text: Malware that encrypts files for ransom
choices.why: That is lessons 7 and 8.

prompt: Match each state of data to where it is watched.

pairs.right: a scan of disks and file servers
the network edge, or the endpoint before encryption
an agent on the endpoint that sees the action

right_distractors: the backup tape in the safe

prompt: Why does most of DLP have to live on the endpoint?
hint: Where is the file still readable?

choices.text: Because network devices are too slow to read files
choices.why: Speed is not the obstacle; encryption is.

choices.text: Because the LGPD forbids inspecting network traffic
choices.why: It forbids nothing of the kind; it asks for proportion.

choices.text: Only there is the file still readable, whatever door it takes
choices.why: Right: uploads and sync are encrypted on the wire; USB and print never cross it.

choices.text: Because endpoints are cheaper to buy than gateways
choices.why: Cost is not the argument the lesson makes.

prompt: Why does the lesson generate its own client list instead of using a copy of real data?

choices.text: Because real CPFs do not pass the check digits
choices.why: Real CPFs pass them; that is what the digits are for.

choices.text: Because the scanner cannot read a file that a spreadsheet exported from a real system
choices.why: It reads the generated CSV, which is exactly that format.

choices.text: Because generated data makes the scanner run faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: A test file with real clients is a leak waiting for a careless copy
choices.why: Right: test data never needs to be real.

prompt: What lets a scanner tell a CPF from any other eleven digits?

choices.text: Its two check digits
choices.why: Right: computed from the first nine, so a random number rarely has them.

choices.text: The dots and the dash in its usual written form
choices.why: CPFs are written without them too, and the pattern accepts both.

choices.text: A list of every issued CPF, downloaded from the Receita Federal
choices.why: No such list is handed out, and it would itself be a vast leak.

choices.text: The first digit, which shows the state of issue
choices.why: Any digit can appear there in a random number.

prompt: About one random eleven-digit number in how many passes both CPF check digits?
hint: Each check digit is right about one time in ten.

prompt: Why do the generated card numbers all start with 9999?

choices.text: Because Luhn's check only works on numbers starting with 9
choices.why: Luhn works on any digits.

choices.text: No card network issues that prefix
choices.why: Right: valid to a scanner, useless as a card.

choices.text: It is the prefix banks reserve for their own test accounts
choices.why: The lesson does not claim that; it only says no network issues it.

choices.text: To make the file easy to sort
choices.why: Sorting is not why.

prompt: Why does scan.py print `881******41` rather than the whole number?

choices.text: Because the terminal cannot show more than five digits
choices.why: It shows the whole count line without trouble.

choices.text: Because the middle digits of a CPF are not checked
choices.why: All nine enter the arithmetic.

choices.text: So its output does not copy the personal data into logs
choices.why: Right: alerts and tickets would otherwise carry the data.

choices.text: To make the scanner faster on large files
choices.why: Masking costs a little time; it does not save any.

prompt: `98765432100` in the order file passed the check. What does that show?

choices.text: A bug in cpf_ok, which should have refused it
choices.why: The arithmetic is right: the number is a valid CPF.

choices.text: A valid number is not always a CPF
choices.why: Right: arithmetic proves the shape, never whose it is.

choices.text: That order numbers are personal data under the LGPD
choices.why: The lesson treats it as a false positive, not as personal data.

choices.text: That the file was saved with the wrong encoding
choices.why: Encoding does not change digits.

prompt: What does exact data match find that the lesson's scanner cannot?

choices.text: Card numbers written with spaces between the groups
choices.why: The scanner's pattern already accepts spaces.

choices.text: Contracts and salary reviews written in sentences
choices.why: Those need labels or fingerprints; EDM matches rows of data.

choices.text: Rows of the real client list, wherever they are
choices.why: Right: real clients, not merely valid numbers.

choices.text: Personal data inside encrypted uploads
choices.why: Nothing reads encrypted traffic without decrypting it.

prompt: What happens to a DLP rule that keeps firing on order numbers?

choices.text: People route round it, and nobody reads its alerts
choices.why: Right: it ends up switched off in practice.

choices.text: It gets more accurate as it sees more of them
choices.why: A pattern learns nothing from firing.

choices.text: The LGPD requires it to be reported to the ANPD
choices.why: A false positive is not an incident.

choices.text: It blocks the order system until somebody fixes it
choices.why: Only if it was set to block, which is why rules start in monitor mode.

prompt: Without the check, how many CPFs did the scanner report in pedidos.txt?
Put a DLP rule's life in the order the lesson recommends.
items: write the rule in monitor mode
read for weeks what it would have blocked
switch it to blocking, with justification allowed

prompt: A rule only counts eleven digits as a CPF when the word CPF is near them. What does it gain and what does it lose?

choices.text: It gains speed and loses the check digits
choices.why: Context is added to the check, not instead of it.

choices.text: Fewer false positives; misses CPFs typed into free text
choices.why: Right: every way of cutting noise misses something.

choices.text: Nothing is lost, because every document labels its CPFs
choices.why: People write CPFs anywhere, labelled or not.

choices.text: It gains exact data match and loses masking
choices.why: Neither is affected by context.

prompt: When does guard.sh check a file?

choices.text: Once an hour, on a schedule set in cron
choices.why: Nothing in it runs on a schedule.

choices.text: When the sync client starts uploading it
choices.why: By then it would be too late; the guard acts before.

choices.text: When somebody runs scan.py by hand
choices.why: The guard runs it, not a person.

choices.text: The moment the file lands in the outbox
choices.why: Right: the kernel tells inotifywait, and the check runs at once.

prompt: The guard held clientes.csv in the outbox, yet `curl -T docs/clientes.csv` sent all of it to trap. Why?

choices.text: Because curl encrypts files before sending them
choices.why: This upload was plain HTTP, and the guard never looks at traffic anyway.

choices.text: The guard watches one folder, and curl read from another
choices.why: Right: an endpoint check covers the actions it hooks and nothing else.

choices.text: Because the guard only checks files owned by root
choices.why: It checked ana's copy of the same file.

choices.text: Because trap is inside the lab, and the guard trusts every machine in the lab
choices.why: Nothing in the guard knows about destinations.

prompt: What does the egress allow-list need to know about a file in order to stop it?

choices.text: Nothing: it only knows where the traffic is going
choices.why: Right, which is its strength and its limit.

choices.text: Whether its content passes the CPF and Luhn checks
choices.why: That is the scanner's job, not the firewall's.

choices.text: The name of the person who is sending it
choices.why: The rule matches addresses and ports, never people.

choices.text: Whether it is encrypted on the way out of the machine
choices.why: It works the same either way.

prompt: With egress.nft loaded, which way out is still open for the client list?

choices.text: An upload to trap on a port other than 8443
choices.why: The rule allows only web's ports and DNS; trap on any port is dropped.

choices.text: An SSH session that desk starts to admin
choices.why: A new connection to admin is not on the list.

choices.text: A form on the portal, which desk is allowed to reach
choices.why: Right: the allowed destination carries any data.

choices.text: None at all
choices.why: The rule knows destinations, and one is allowed.

prompt: The scanner finds twenty card numbers in a spreadsheet on a workstation. What does the LGPD's necessity principle make of that?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the file never leaves the firm
choices.why: Holding data the purpose does not need is the finding.

choices.text: A finding: why does the firm keep them at all?
choices.why: Right: the cheapest data to protect is the data deleted.

choices.text: A reason to encrypt the spreadsheet and keep it
choices.why: Encryption protects data the firm needs; first ask if it does.

choices.text: An incident to report to the ANPD within the day
choices.why: Nothing has leaked; it is a question about keeping.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson ask of a DLP deployment that watches staff? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Tell people the monitoring exists
choices.why: And people who know stop making the mistake.

choices.text: Keep only what the job needs, such as counts and masked examples
choices.why: Proportion, as the guard does.

choices.text: Keep a full copy of every file each employee sends
choices.why: That would be a second copy of everything worth protecting.

choices.text: Limit who reads the logs and how long they are kept
choices.why: The logs are among the most sensitive files.

prompt: An employee pastes a client's CPF into a chat window in the browser. Which of the lesson's controls sees it?

choices.text: The guard, because the browser saves a copy in the outbox
choices.why: Nothing is written to the outbox.

choices.text: The egress rule, if the chat site is on the allow-list
choices.why: If it is on the list it is allowed, and the rule never sees content.

choices.text: Neither
choices.why: Right: a paste is an action only a product's agent hooks.

choices.text: Both, one after the other
choices.why: Neither hooks a paste.
